entries.note: The page does not say what `from` holds for a message with an empty reverse path (a bounce). Podbay answers only something that is one whole address, so an empty value, `<>` and anything else get no automatic reply (test/workerd/auto-reply.test.ts).

entries.relies: Email Routing puts its own `Authentication-Results` field in front of the message. Podbay reads the first such field through `message.headers` and keeps it only when its identifier is exactly `mx.cloudflare.net`.

entries.relies: A raw message posted to `/cdn-cgi/local/email?from=…&to=…` on the local server is delivered to the `email` handler.

entries.relies: A Durable Object can set one alarm at a time. The mailbox object keeps every time it waits for in rows and sets its one alarm to the earliest (ADR-0016, decision 17); snooze (ADR-0010) adds its times to the same function.
entries.evidence: Each Durable Object is able to schedule a single alarm at a time by calling `setAlarm()`.
entries.note: The same page: `Alarms have guaranteed at-least-once execution and are retried automatically when the alarm() handler throws.` Since ADR-0016 the mailbox object has an alarm: outgoing mail leaves from it.

entries.relies: One Durable Object stores at most 10 GB, so raw messages and attachments live in R2.
entries.evidence: 10 GB on Workers Paid, or 1 GB on the Free plan
entries.note: 10 GB holds on Workers Paid only. On the Free plan one Durable Object stores 1 GB and the account 5 GB in total.

entries.relies: A string, a blob or a table row in a Durable Object is at most 8 MB. A message whose text would not fit is filed with its original alone (`unparsed: too_large`).

The local runtime took a string of 8,000,001 bytes and refused one of 8,388,608 (`SQLITE_TOOBIG`; tried in test/workerd on 2026-11-17). Podbay treats more than 8,000,000 bytes of text as too large, and a refusal by the database the same way.

entries.evidence: | Maximum bound parameters per query | 100 |

entries.relies: The MCP endpoint is `createMcpHandler` from `agents/mcp/server` around an MCP SDK v2 server built for one request: no Durable Object and no protocol session, so nothing outlives the key check made for that request.

entries.relies: The handler refuses a browser Origin that is not allowed; Podbay allows only the hostname the request came to and removes the CORS headers (`corsOptions: false`), so no other site's page can use the endpoint. Clients that send no Origin still work.

entries.note: The page says a custom domain with wildcard CORS must set `allowedHostnames` and `allowedOriginHostnames` itself; Podbay sets the Origin list on every request and sends no CORS headers.

entries.relies: D1 has SQLite's JSON functions. `json_patch` lays a change over a person's stored choices in one statement: a key of the change replaces, a `null` removes, every other key stays. `json_valid` and `json_extract` guard a document that cannot be read or is of a later version (ADR-0012).
entries.evidence: Uses a JSON [MergePatch ↗︎](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7396) approach to merge the provided patch into the target JSON object.
entries.note: The page gives no example for `json_patch`. The same table, of `json_valid(json)`: "Returns 0 (false) for invalid JSON, and 1 (true) for valid JSON." That a `null` removes a key, that a key the change does not name stays, and that two merges at once both hold was tried on the local runtime (test/workerd/choices.test.ts).

entries.relies: D1 runs SQLite's SQL, so one `insert … on conflict … do update … where` statement makes a person's row or merges into it, and changes nothing when the stored document is of a later version.
entries.evidence: D1 is compatible with most SQLite's SQL convention since it leverages SQLite's query engine.
entries.note: The source is narrower than the code: it says "most" and does not name the upsert clause. The statement is proven on the local runtime (test/workerd/choices.test.ts: a first write, a merge, a refused merge that changes no row); `RETURNING` is not used, the merged document is read in the same batch.

entries.relies: A string or a row in D1 is at most 2 MB. A person's choices are one small document: its keys and values come from closed lists, and a request that changes it is at most 4 KiB (ADR-0012).
entries.evidence: | Maximum string, `BLOB` or table row size | 2,000,000 bytes (2 MB) |
entries.note: The same table: "| Queries per Worker invocation (read [subrequest limits](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/#subrequests)) | 1000 (Workers Paid) / 50 (Free) |"; a change to the choices is one batch, which counts as one query.

entries.relies: The mailbox object takes a connection with `acceptWebSocket` and not with `accept()`, so it can leave memory while the connection stays open (ADR-0013, decision 1).
entries.evidence: which allows a Durable Object to be removed from memory to save costs while keeping its WebSockets connected.

entries.relies: While the object is not in memory its connections stay open, and what it held in memory is gone when it wakes: the counters are stored and nothing about a connection is kept in memory.
entries.evidence: When an event arrives, the Durable Object is re-initialized and its `constructor` runs
entries.note: The same page: "Clients remain connected while the Durable Object is not in memory" and "In-memory state is reset". Shown locally with `evictDurableObject` (test/workerd/live.test.ts); not shown on Cloudflare's network.

entries.relies: A connection carries the id of its person as a tag, and the object finds a person's connections again with `getWebSockets(tag)`. The object refuses an id longer than a tag may be.
entries.evidence: Each tag is a maximum of 256 characters and there can be at most 10 tags associated with a WebSocket.
entries.note: No page says in words that tags outlast hibernation; `getWebSockets` and `getTags` are documented as part of the Hibernation API. test/workerd/live.test.ts shows it in the local runtime after `evictDurableObject`: a connection is found by its tag and closed for the right person. Not shown on Cloudflare's network.

entries.relies: A connection keeps, as its attachment, when the guard allowed it and the message it was last sent. Both are there after the object slept, so an old connection is closed and the same state is never sent twice.
entries.evidence: Serialized attachments persist through hibernation as long as the WebSocket remains healthy
entries.note: The same list: "Maximum serialized size is 16,384 bytes"; an attachment here is a number and a message of at most 256 bytes.

entries.relies: The app says `ping` and the platform answers `pong` without waking the mailbox object. The pair is set in the constructor, as the platform's example does.
entries.evidence: If a request is received matching the provided request then the auto-response will be returned without waking WebSockets in hibernation and incurring billable duration charges.
entries.note: "Both request and response are limited to 2,048 characters each."

entries.relies: Nothing yet: the app pings once a minute whether or not an auto-answered ping is billed as a received message. At twenty to one it would be three requests an hour for an open tab (ADR-0013, Consequences).
entries.evidence: needs verification: the page says an auto-response is not charged wall-clock time, in a footnote on duration; it does not say whether one counts as a received message.
entries.note: The footnote: "Application level auto-response messages handled by" `state.setWebSocketAutoResponse()` "will not incur additional wall-clock time, and so they will not be charged." Cannot be tested locally: billing is not simulated. To settle on a real account, from the Durable Objects request metrics of an idle mailbox with one open tab.

entries.relies: Opening a connection is one request to the object; what the object sends costs nothing; what it receives is counted at twenty to one. The app sends nothing but `ping`, and the object closes a connection that sends anything else.
entries.evidence: For compute requests billing-only, a 20:1 ratio is applied to incoming WebSocket messages to factor in smaller messages for real-time communication.
entries.note: The same footnote: "A request is needed to create a WebSocket connection. There is no charge for outgoing WebSocket messages".

entries.relies: The mailbox object holds no timer and takes no WebSocket with `accept()`, so it can sleep with its connections open: the five minutes of a connection are checked when it is awake for another reason, and bursts are evened out in the app.
entries.evidence: After 10 seconds of no incoming request or event, and all the above conditions satisfied, the Durable Object will transition into the **hibernated** state.
entries.note: The conditions above it: no `setTimeout`/`setInterval` callback, no unfinished I/O or `waitUntil` promise, "No WebSocket standard API is used", no request still being processed.

entries.relies: The object closes a connection with `close(1008, reason)` and does not answer a close itself: with the compatibility date in `wrangler.jsonc` the runtime completes the close handshake.
entries.evidence: With this flag active, you no longer need to call `close()` in your `close` event handler. The runtime handles the close handshake automatically.
entries.note: The flag is `web_socket_auto_reply_to_close`, on by default from compatibility date 2026-04-07 (the state API page says the same).

entries.relies: A mailbox takes at most 200 connections (ADR-0013, decision 20), far under what one object may hold.
entries.evidence: The WebSocket Hibernation API permits a maximum of 32,768 WebSocket connections per Durable Object

entries.relies: A message the object receives may be large; the object reads none of it. Anything but `ping`, which the platform answers, closes the connection, whatever its size.
entries.evidence: | WebSocket message size | 32 MiB (only for received messages) |

entries.relies: A deploy, a runtime update or a reset of the object can close connections, so the app reconnects by itself and never trusts the connection to be there.
entries.evidence: By default, Durable Objects defer code updates for up to 300 seconds (5 minutes) to give in-flight requests time to finish.
entries.note: The WebSockets page: "Connections accepted with the WebSocket Hibernation API remain connected when a Durable Object adopts new code after hibernating."

entries.relies: The Worker checks the handshake (the guard) and hands the object a request; the object's `fetch` accepts the connection and its response, with status 101, is what the Worker returns.
entries.evidence: Validate requests in your Worker to avoid billing for invalid requests against a Durable Object.
entries.note: The page's Worker passes the browser's own request on; Podbay builds a new one, so that no cookie or header of the browser reaches the object (ADR-0013, decision 10). The page's example answers a request that is not an upgrade with 426, as the guard does.

entries.relies: A counter is moved in the same turn as the change it counts, with no `await` of I/O between them, so both are stored or neither (ADR-0013, decision 5). The same holds for the alarm: a message is taken, taken back or given a new time and the alarm is set in the same turn (ADR-0016, decision 17).
entries.evidence: Any series of write operations with no intervening `await` will automatically be submitted atomically

entries.relies: The mailbox object asks SQLite for `total_changes()` before and after each of its methods, to know whether the call changed a row. The function is on the runtime's list of allowed SQL functions.
entries.evidence: "total_changes"_kj,
entries.note: The SQL API page (updated 2026-09-21) points at this file and commit: "Refer to the [source code ↗︎](…) for the full list of supported functions." The quoted line is in `ALLOWED_SQLITE_FUNCTIONS`. test/workerd/live-signal.test.ts runs it in the local runtime: a read leaves it as it was, a write moves it.

entries.relies: Nothing: the app says `ping` once a minute and reconnects when a connection is gone, so it does not depend on how long a silent connection is kept.
entries.evidence: needs verification: no page read on 2026-11-17 says how long a WebSocket to a Worker may stay silent before the network closes it.
entries.note: Locally (Chrome, the built app, the local runtime) a connection on which nothing was said for 130 seconds stayed open and was still told (test/e2e/live.spec.ts runs it with 65 seconds). That says nothing about Cloudflare's network.

entries.relies: The Workers-runtime tests put a mailbox object out of memory with its connections open, to show what a connection keeps through sleep.
entries.evidence: `evictDurableObject(stub:DurableObjectStub, options?:DurableObjectEvictionOptions)`: Promise\<void>

entries.relies: The mailbox object's `alarm()` runs when the alarm's time comes, one run at a time for one object. A run that finds a message handed over already does nothing for it.
entries.evidence: Only one instance of `alarm()` will ever run at a given time per Durable Object instance.

entries.relies: A handler that throws is tried again six times and then not at all until an alarm is set again. So the mailbox's handler catches its own errors and always sets the next alarm (ADR-0016, decision 18).
entries.evidence: Retries are performed using exponential backoff starting at a 2 second delay from the first failure with up to 6 retries allowed.

entries.relies: A handler can start over on another machine. The handover of a message is therefore a compare-and-set written before the service is called: a run that starts over finds `sending` and hands nothing over again (ADR-0016, decision 5).
entries.evidence: Following a short delay, the `alarm()` handler will run from the beginning on the other machine.

entries.relies: An alarm can be late by up to a minute. A late alarm makes the undo window longer, never shorter: what decides is the state of the row, not the clock (ADR-0016, decision 11).
entries.evidence: will usually execute within a few milliseconds after the set time, but can be delayed by up to a minute due to maintenance or failures while failover takes place.

entries.relies: An alarm set to a time that has come runs at once. A run that leaves mail due (more than ten messages) sets the alarm to their time and is run again.
entries.evidence: If `setAlarm()` is called with a time equal to or before `Date.now()`, the alarm will be scheduled for asynchronous execution in the immediate future.

entries.relies: Whenever the object wakes it asks whether an alarm is set, and sets one when something waits and none is. An alarm that has not started counts as set, so a wake for the alarm itself sets no second one.
entries.evidence: The alarm is considered to be set if it has not started, or if it has failed and any retry has not begun.
entries.note: The alarms page adds that `getAlarm` answers `null` while a handler is running unless `setAlarm` was called since it started; the handler always calls `setAlarm` or `deleteAlarm` at its end.

entries.relies: The constructor runs before the alarm handler when the object was asleep. The constructor of the mailbox object sets an alarm only after asking whether one is set.
entries.evidence: If you wish to call `setAlarm` inside the constructor of a Durable Object, ensure that you are first checking whether an alarm has already been set.

entries.relies: An alarm can be lost: one held for more than seven days while a spending limit blocks the account's objects is deleted. The rows are still there, the alarm is set again at the next wake, and a message 24 hours past its time does not leave (ADR-0016, decisions 15 and 18).
entries.evidence: An alarm scheduled more than seven days ago is deleted while held.

entries.relies: A run of the alarm lets at most ten messages leave and waits at most 60 seconds for the service's answer to each, so it ends inside the fifteen minutes a handler may run.
entries.evidence: Alarm handler invocations have a maximum wall time of 15 minutes.

entries.relies: Deleting a mailbox deletes its alarm with its rows, so a deleted mailbox sends nothing (ADR-0016, decision 21). The compatibility date is later than 2026-02-24; `purge` also calls `deleteAlarm()` first.
entries.evidence: For Workers with a compatibility date of `2026-02-24` or later, `deleteAll()` also deletes any active [alarm](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/alarms/).

entries.relies: The handover of a message (`waiting` to `sending`) is on disk before the sending service hears of it: the platform holds outgoing messages until the write is confirmed, and Podbay also waits for `sync()` before the call.
entries.evidence: By default, the system will pause outgoing network messages from the Durable Object until all previous writes have been confirmed flushed to disk.

entries.relies: `ctx.storage.sync()` resolves when the writes made so far are on disk. The mailbox waits for it between the handover and the call to the sending service.
entries.evidence: Synchronizes any pending writes to disk.

entries.relies: The mailbox object has the Worker's bindings. Since ADR-0016 it uses three of them: the send binding, the bucket (the files of a message that leaves) and the index (whether the mailbox is still there and its sender may still send).
entries.evidence: `env` contains the environment bindings available to this Durable Object, as defined in your Wrangler configuration.

entries.relies: The alarm handler, and the step that files an arrival when it asks whether the automatic reply is owed, read the mailbox's address from `ctx.id.name`: the object is named after the address in the index, and nothing in a row says which mailbox it is. Without a name nothing leaves and no reply is made.
entries.evidence: The `name` property is also available on `ctx.id` inside the Durable Object when the caller uses `idFromName()` or `getByName()`.
entries.note: The page: the name is `undefined` when the caller used `idFromString()`, and for alarms created before 2026-03-15. Podbay reaches a mailbox only by `idFromName` (`getMailboxStub`, the guard). Seen to hold in the local runtime on 2026-11-18 (`test/workerd/sending.test.ts`).

entries.relies: A refusal of the sending service carries one of 24 codes. Three read as "not now" and are tried again (`E_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, `E_INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`, `E_EMAIL_SENDING_NOT_READY`); every other code is final (ADR-0016, decisions 6 and 8).
entries.evidence: Email Service errors have a `code` property. The following error codes may be returned when sending emails:
entries.note: The table's own words for the three: "Sending rate or concurrent send limit reached", "Email Service temporarily unavailable", "Domain onboarding has not finished. Retry the send later". The page says to retry of the third only; reading the first two as "not now" is ADR-0016's. `E_DAILY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` ("Daily sending quota reached") is final. `E_DELIVERY_FAILED` does not say whether another recipient was reached.

entries.relies: An argument of the wrong shape is refused with a `TypeError` that has no code: the service did not take the message. Podbay records it as a message that does not fit (`limits`), never as `unknown`.
entries.evidence: If the argument to `send()` does not match the [interface](#interface), `send()` throws a `TypeError` without a `code` property.

entries.relies: `send()` takes no idempotency key and the service gives every message it takes an id of its own, so Podbay cannot ask whether a handover that got no answer arrived. Such a message is `failed` with `unknown` and is never handed over again (ADR-0016, decision 7).
entries.evidence: messageId: string; // Unique email ID
entries.note: A fact of absence: the interface on the page lists `to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `from`, `subject`, `html`, `text`, `replyTo`, `attachments` and `headers`, and names no key of that kind. Read again when the page changes.

entries.relies: The Workers-runtime tests run a mailbox's alarm by hand after ageing its rows, instead of waiting for time.
entries.evidence: Immediately runs and removes the Durable Object pointed to by `stub`'s alarm if one is scheduled.
entries.note: Seen on 2026-11-18: an alarm whose time has come also runs by itself in the test runtime, so a test that must see one run sets a time that has not come and runs it by hand.

entries.relies: The Workers-runtime tests put a send binding of their own into a mailbox object, which answers what a test says and counts every call; no test reaches a sending service.
entries.evidence: Runs the provided `callback` inside the Durable Object that corresponds to the provided `stub`.

entries.relies: The sending service takes `Auto-Submitted` in the `headers` map. An automatic reply (ADR-0008, decision 9) is handed over with `Auto-Submitted: auto-replied`, so that no program answers it.
entries.evidence: Values include `no`, `auto-generated`, `auto-replied`, and extension tokens.
entries.note: Not seen on Cloudflare's network: the automatic reply is tried with a send binding of the tests (test/workerd/auto-reply.test.ts).

entries.relies: A header the service does not list refuses the whole send. Podbay hands over three and no other: `In-Reply-To` and `References` for an answer a person wrote, `Auto-Submitted` for an automatic reply.
entries.evidence: Email Service rejects the entire send request if it contains a disallowed header.

entries.relies: A Worker may be 64 MiB uncompressed on both plans, with no limit on its compressed size, so every module can live in the one Worker (ADR-0018, decision 1).
entries.evidence: There is no compressed size limit. Only the uncompressed bundle size counts.

entries.relies: A Worker has one collection of static assets, so the single-page app is served by one Worker; a second Worker would not serve it (ADR-0018).
entries.evidence: Only one collection of static assets can be configured in each Worker.

entries.relies: A call from one Worker to another through a service binding counts against the calling request's subrequests and its 32 Worker invocations. ADR-0018 keeps every module in one Worker, so no module call pays this.
entries.evidence: A single request has a maximum of 32 Worker invocations, and each call to a Service binding counts towards this limit.
entries.note: The same page says service bindings "don't increase costs"; the pricing page says such calls "do not incur additional request fees".

entries.relies: A Durable Object class defined in one Worker can be bound from another by naming that Worker. ADR-0018 does not use it: every class stays in the one Worker.
entries.evidence: The name of the Worker where the Durable Object is defined, if it is external to this Worker.

entries.relies: A migration tag names a migration that has been applied, once per environment. The tags `v1` and `v2` stay as they are through any move of files (ADR-0018, decision 3).
entries.evidence: Migration tags are treated like unique names and are used to determine which migrations have already been applied.
entries.note: Neither page says whether an applied tag may be edited or removed; ADR-0018 treats them as never changed.

entries.relies: Moving a class's stored objects to a class of another Worker is a transfer migration. ADR-0018 makes no transfer part of the move.
entries.evidence: Transfer migrations are used to transfer stored Durable Objects between two Durable Object classes
entries.note: The page on `exports` says a transfer is "a multi-deploy flow" because "two Workers must coordinate".

entries.relies: Deleting a class deletes every object of it with its data. No delete migration is part of the move (ADR-0018, decision 3).
entries.evidence: Running a Delete migration will delete all Durable Objects associated with the deleted class

entries.relies: Declaring classes with `exports` cannot be undone once deployed. Podbay keeps the `migrations` list; a change to `exports` needs its own record (ADR-0018).
entries.evidence: Once a Worker has been deployed with `exports`, subsequent deploys cannot return to the legacy `migrations` array.

entries.relies: With more than one Worker in the Vite plugin, every request goes through the entry Worker and only it is deployed by `wrangler deploy`; each other Worker is deployed on its own. One reason ADR-0018 keeps one Worker.
entries.evidence: All requests are routed through your entry Worker.

entries.relies: In the Workers test integration, a Worker beside the one under test must be compiled to JavaScript and cannot use `cloudflare:test`, which the tier-3 tests rely on. One reason ADR-0018 keeps one Worker.
entries.evidence: Cannot have TypeScript entrypoints. You must compile auxiliary Workers to JavaScript first.
entries.note: The same list says auxiliary Workers "Cannot access the cloudflare:test module."

entries.relies: A Worker can resolve DNS with `node:dns`, over DNS over HTTPS to 1.1.1.1, each query a subrequest, with nothing to switch on at Podbay's compatibility date. So a Domains screen can read a domain's records without an account token (ADR-0018, decision 9).
entries.evidence: You can use node:dns for name resolution via DNS over HTTPS using Cloudflare DNS at 1.1.1.1.
entries.note: All node:dns functions are available except lookupService. Nothing uses it yet.

entries.relies: The runtime takes every HTTP method but CONNECT on a Request. Whether WebDAV's and CalDAV's methods reach a Worker through Cloudflare's network is not stated, and the HTTP library under the runtime does not list MKCALENDAR. ADR-0018 lets no first slice depend on them until a test on a real custom domain shows which arrive.
entries.evidence: In Workers, all HTTP request methods are supported, except for `CONNECT`.
entries.note: The method list `KJ_HTTP_FOR_EACH_REQUEST_METHOD` in capnproto's `c++/src/kj/compat/http.h` (branch v2, read 2026-11-19) has PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, LOCK, MKCOL and REPORT and not MKCALENDAR; the commit workerd pins was not read.

entries.relies: The runtime's Web Crypto lists ECDH, HKDF, AES-GCM and ECDSA, the operations Web Push needs (RFC 8291, RFC 8292). Nothing uses them yet (ADR-0018, decision 7).
entries.evidence: Workers implements all operations of the WebCrypto standard
entries.note: The page does not name the P-256 curve both RFCs require; that is not verified, and is tested before push is built.

entries.relies: One Worker can answer on several custom domains, so a hostname of its own for content people upload does not by itself ask for a second Worker (ADR-0018, decision 9). The Worker then answers by hostname.
entries.evidence: You can add multiple Custom Domains.

entries.relies: D1 applies the files of the one migrations folder in the order of the version number in their names, and records the applied ones in the `d1_migrations` table. So every module's migrations share one numbered sequence, and a number once applied is never reused or moved (ADR-0018, decision 1).
entries.evidence: Every migration file in the `migrations` folder has a specified version number in the filename. Files are listed in sequential order.
entries.note: The page records applied migrations "in the `d1_migrations` table found in your database"; it does not say in so many words that an applied migration is never applied again, only that wrangler lists and applies the unapplied ones.
